solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Just avoided defeat as ringer prevented goal-scoring?

definitions.meaning: rescued at the last moment, as a boxer on the canvas is spared when the round ends
read literally: a shot was kept out (saved) by a bell, the thing that rings

explanation.surface: A football team narrowly escapes losing because some ringer stopped the other side from scoring.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading takes the idiom word by word: a goalkeeper 'saves', and the 'ringer' (normally a cheat fielded under a false name) is a bell.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom from boxing, where the end-of-round bell rescues a fighter about to be counted out.

clue.text: In the middle of clearing, angry, sick, old scaly creature

indicators.note: the central letters of the word clearing are taken, its middle pair

parts.note: angry means mad
sick means ill

explanation.surface: In a forest clearing, an old, sick and angry reptile stands in the middle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the middle of' looks like scene-setting but picks the central two letters of the eight-letter 'clearing', AR.
explanation.definitionFit: This South American mammal is covered in bony plates, making it a scaly animal.

clue.text: Duck I left for large tree

indicators.note: the letter I departs and the abbreviation for large takes its place, so one letter is swapped for another

parts.note: the eider is a sea duck
taken as written
L is the standard abbreviation for large, as on clothing labels

explanation.surface: A duck and I abandon our spot in favour of a large tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left' is not the direction L here: 'I left for large' means the I leaves to make way for L.
explanation.definitionFit: The elder is a small deciduous tree or shrub bearing elderflowers and elderberries.

clue.text: Top of calyx in flatter flower

indicators.note: the opening letter of calyx is placed inside the phrasal verb for flatter

parts.note: to butter up is to flatter someone

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down clue is its first letter, so calyx gives its opening letter

explanation.surface: A botanical note: the tip of a calyx sits inside a flatter kind of flower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flatter' reads as an adjective (less curved) but is the verb, giving BUTTER UP.
explanation.definitionFit: The buttercup is a common yellow wild plant, a familiar meadow bloom.

clue.text: Journeys would be nonsense if direction were changed

indicators.note: one compass point in the word for nonsense, east, is exchanged for another, south

parts.note: tripe is a colloquial word for nonsense

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that their travels would be pointless if the route were altered.
explanation.walkthrough: The compass points are E (east) and S (south): swapping one for the other is the 'change of direction'.
explanation.definitionFit: Trips are outings or excursions, so the plural noun matches the plural journeys.

clue.text: Leeds turn round the final score

indicators.note: turning things round reorders them, so the letters of the two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A football report: Leeds United come back to change the final score.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn round' looks like the anagram signal, but 'turn' is part of the fodder and 'round' alone signals; the definition is 'final score', with 'the' joining.
explanation.definitionFit: The end result is the final outcome of something, as the closing score is of a match.

clue.text: Eastern group capture current novelist

indicators.note: the group takes the symbol for current inside it, as a captor holds a prisoner

parts.note: a lot is a group or batch
I is the physics symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: An eastern gang seizes a novelist who is in the news.
explanation.walkthrough: 'current' is not an adjective meaning topical but the physicist's I.
explanation.definitionFit: George Eliot was the pen name of Mary Ann Evans, author of Middlemarch.

clue.text: Reasonable food for slimmers consumed by soldier? Quite the opposite

indicators.note: one piece is swallowed inside another
the reverse of what was said: the soldier goes inside the diet food, not the other way round

parts.note: lo-cal, short for low-calorie, describes slimming food
GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: A soldier tucks into some diet food, or rather it swallows him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quite the opposite' flips 'consumed by', so the diet food swallows the soldier rather than the reverse.
explanation.definitionFit: Logical and reasonable are synonyms, both describing sound thinking.

clue.text: Poem about horse with alligator skin — I don't think that works!

indicators.note: the poem goes around the letter for horse

parts.note: an ode is a lyric poem
H is slang for heroin, which is also called horse

indicators.note: the skin of a word is its outside letters, first and last

explanation.surface: A dismissive critic reads a poem about a horse wearing alligator hide and declares it a failure.
explanation.walkthrough: Horse is slang for heroin, abbreviated H; the 'skin' of alligator is AR.
explanation.definitionFit: An interjection of mild dismay, the kind of thing said when a plan looks doomed.

clue.text: Sweaty Chinese President stupid to return

parts.note: Hu Jintao was President of China from 2003 to 2013

indicators.note: returning means the word for stupid is read backwards

parts.note: dim means stupid

explanation.surface: A sweating Chinese leader is daft enough to come back.
explanation.definitionFit: Humid air is damp and muggy, the kind of weather that leaves you sweaty.

clue.text: Time to be going, if this is what you're doing with your thumbs?

definitions.text: what you're doing with your thumbs

parts.note: widdling is a childish British word for urinating, in the sense of 'going' to the toilet

explanation.surface: If you're idly turning your thumbs over, it's probably time to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be going' looks like 'leaving'; the euphemism is the toilet sense, WIDDLING. 'Widdle' is British nursery slang for wee.
explanation.definitionFit: Twiddling your thumbs means rotating them idly round each other while bored or waiting.

clue.text: Back part to defend or secure

indicators.note: only part of the words defend or secure is used, a stretch running across them

explanation.surface: A defender's instruction: the back line exists to protect or make safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' is not the defence but the verb: to back is to support.
explanation.definitionFit: To back a proposal or a candidate is to endorse it, giving public support.

clue.text: Doubting Simon starts to have reaction with mushroom

definitions.note: the dictionary also lists this word as an adjective, an older form of sceptical

indicators.note: the start of the name Simon is its first letter

parts.note: the cep is an edible mushroom, the porcini
a tic is an involuntary twitch or reaction

explanation.surface: A doubting Simon suddenly reacts to some mushroom, like a dubious foodie.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface echoes 'Doubting Thomas'; 'starts' gives only Simon's S.
explanation.definitionFit: Being disinclined to believe claims without evidence is the core of a doubting outlook.

clue.text: Last remaining piece of dereliction

indicators.note: the solution is a piece taken out of the word dereliction, a run of its letters

explanation.surface: An old ruin leaves just one surviving fragment.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition and the extraction share 'piece': a piece of dereliction is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A relic is something surviving from an earlier time, a remnant left over.

clue.text: Type of dating Ms Palmer-Tomkinson has no time for — it's saucy

parts.note: carbon dating is a method of finding the age of organic remains

indicators.note: the socialite's first name loses the letter for time

parts.note: Tara Palmer-Tomkinson was a British socialite and TV personality

explanation.surface: A gossip item: the socialite has no time for a certain kind of dating, which is rather racy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dating' sounds romantic but is the archaeologists' CARBON dating; 'saucy' means served in a sauce.
explanation.definitionFit: Carbonara is a pasta sauce of egg, cheese and bacon, so a dish of it is literally saucy.

clue.text: This country's surrounded by foul chlorine haze of several hues

indicators.note: the word for this country's sits inside the mixed letters
a haze blurs and jumbles things, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: Cl is the chemical symbol for chlorine
our, as in belonging to this country

explanation.surface: Britain lies under a smoggy cloud of chlorine glowing in many colours.
explanation.walkthrough: 'haze' scrambles the foul letters with chlorine's symbol into COLFUL, and 'surrounded by' sets this country's word in its middle.
explanation.definitionFit: Colourful means full of bright and varied colours, multicoloured.

clue.text: Editorial about Scottish town preacher

indicators.note: the editorial goes around the town's name

parts.note: a leader is a newspaper's editorial article
Ayr is a town on the west coast of Scotland

explanation.surface: A newspaper editorial concerns a preacher in a Scottish town.
explanation.definitionFit: A lay reader is a layperson licensed to conduct some church services and give sermons.

clue.text: Refined oil, in fact, is imaginary

indicators.note: refined oil has been processed and changed, so the letters are reworked

explanation.surface: Someone claims processed oil is actually an illusion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in fact' reads as a filler phrase but its letters are fodder with OIL.
explanation.definitionFit: Fictional means invented, existing only in stories rather than reality.

clue.text: Happy George misses PE, involved in another lesson

indicators.note: the gym lesson is skipped, so its letters are taken from the pool
involved means tangled up, so the remaining letters are rearranged

parts.note: physical education, the school gym lesson

explanation.surface: George is glad to skip gym class and gets caught up in a different lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove P and E from HAPPYGEORGE and 'involved' rearranges what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Geography is a school subject, so it is a further lesson besides physical education.

clue.text: Clever thing to do with CO2 possibly short of band to restrict intake

parts.note: carbon dioxide is one example of a gas

indicators.note: the word for clever thing is cut short, losing its final letter

parts.note: a trick is a clever move

explanation.surface: A neat stunt with carbon dioxide almost replaces surgery to limit eating.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the adjective in 'gastric band', the surgical ring fitted round the stomach to limit how much is eaten.
explanation.definitionFit: Gastric means relating to the stomach, as in the stomach-band operation for weight loss.

clue.text: Yacht's beginning to change direction before getting slightly sticky

indicators.note: the sailing word is placed ahead of the yacht's first letter

parts.note: to tack is to change a sailing boat's course

indicators.note: the beginning of the word yacht is its first letter

explanation.surface: A yacht starts to turn just before its deck gets a bit gluey.
explanation.definitionFit: Tacky describes paint or glue not quite dry, still faintly adhesive.

clue.text: Agreements being partially overturned displeases Seychelles

indicators.note: overturned says the hidden letters are read backwards
partially says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Islanders in the Seychelles are annoyed when their votes in favour get overturned.
explanation.walkthrough: The draft's definition 'Agreements being' would not stand in for a plural noun; 'being' is a link word joining definition to wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Each yes is an assent, so plural affirmative replies are agreements.

clue.text: Marine child's tempers

parts.note: sea, as in of the ocean
son's, a child's, with the possessive giving the final letter

explanation.surface: A sailor's son has a fiery temper, perhaps salty like the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tempers' is the verb: to season or temper is to moderate or toughen, as timber is seasoned.
explanation.definitionFit: To season something is to temper it, moderating it or making it hardy through exposure.

clue.text: Type of boat port keeps for poet

indicators.note: the port holds the boat's letter within it

parts.note: Aden is a port city in Yemen
a U-boat is a German submarine

explanation.surface: A harbour retains a certain vessel for a visiting poet.
explanation.definitionFit: W. H. Auden was an Anglo-American poet, author of Funeral Blues.

clue.text: Peculiar culture talk finishes after quiet film

indicators.note: the last letters come after the word for quiet

parts.note: sh is the instruction to be quiet

indicators.note: the finishes of the three words are their last letters

explanation.surface: An odd lecture about culture follows a silent film.
explanation.definitionFit: Shrek is the 2001 animated film about a grumpy ogre.

clue.text: Draws on English parliamentarian's evidence of drinking bouts?

indicators.note: the word for draws comes on after, following the other pieces

parts.note: MP is a Member of Parliament
ties are drawn games

explanation.surface: A cartoonist sketches an English MP's evidence of heavy drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Draws' is not sketches but drawn matches, TIES.
explanation.definitionFit: Empty bottles left behind are the telltale sign of a session of drinking, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Hot Asian item under pressure regularly in big league

indicators.note: in this down clue the chosen letters sit beneath the abbreviation for pressure

parts.note: P is the physics abbreviation for pressure

indicators.note: taking letters at regular intervals, every second one of the words big league

explanation.surface: A spicy Asian dish is under pressure regularly in the top league.
explanation.definitionFit: Pilau is spiced rice cooked in stock, a dish from South and Central Asia served hot.

clue.text: Strikingly-topped ditch cleared out with dry grass surrounding

indicators.note: the grass goes around the other pieces

parts.note: a reed is a tall grass

indicators.note: the word ditch is emptied, leaving only its outside letters

parts.note: to air laundry is to dry it

explanation.surface: A ditch is dug out and surrounded by dried grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cleared out' leaves DH from ditch; 'dry' is the verb AIR.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with ginger hair has a head that stands out, hence a strikingly coloured top.

clue.text: Attack backed, for example, points regularly awarded to British Eurovision song

indicators.note: backed means the pieces are read backwards

parts.words: points regularly awarded to British Eurovision song
parts.note: nul points, French for zero points, a score British Eurovision entries have famously received

explanation.surface: A jibe at Britain's Eurovision record: the usual zero score attacked.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Eurovision Song Contest a song scoring nothing gets 'nul points', and the UK has done so more than once.
explanation.definitionFit: A lunge is a sudden forward thrust, as with a sword, so it is an attack.

clue.text: Grumpily showing lousy mess on tin ship

indicators.note: the jumbled letters come on after the tin and ship

parts.note: a tin is a can
a tanker is a ship carrying oil

indicators.note: a mess is a jumble, so the letters of lousy are rearranged

explanation.surface: A grumpy sailor complains of a lousy mess hall on a tin-can ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mess' suggests a ship's dining room; here it rearranges LOUSY into OUSLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Cantankerously means in a bad-tempered, quarrelsome way, the same as grumpily.
